The PDF has no author code/project URL; its only external URL is a Hugging Face reward-model footnote on p.10. gh repo view confirmed the four automatic candidates are paper aggregators or an arXiv daily tracker, and gh search repos for the title returned no repository. paper_style.palette_strategy: Figures 2–9 use a small orange/green/purple palette for τ and add blue/red for q or K sweeps. Figure 1 uses deep blue for illustrative flow, while Figures 10–11 use blue only for dashed scope boundaries. Palette semantics are local and no cross-figure color dictionary is provided.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Figure 1 combines a PDF Form with 52 embedded RGB/soft-mask illustration objects. Figures 2–11 and Table 1 are primarily vector paths, text, math glyphs, and rules; no independent raster object appears on their pages in pdfimages -list.
paper_style.style_consistency: The paper maintains compact page-width figures, repeated grid/legend/line conventions, and a serif Computer Modern/Nimbus Roman typography family. Figure internals use very small 3–4 pt ticks/legends, while the algorithm diagrams use larger boxes and formulas; the visual grammar is stable but not fully self-describing.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Two examples of online learning and equilibrium computation with ranking feedback. In (a), an online platform recommends food options to a customer at each timestep and receives a ranking over the proposed items, which it uses to improve recommendation quality. In (b), an online dating app recommends potential matches; users rank the suggested candidates, and the platform leverages these rankings to learn matching equilibria over time.

color.semantic_mapping: Deep blue marks containers and information flow; black/white carry icons and text; the remaining colors belong to illustrative food/person icons rather than data series.

encodings.text: timestep, platform, proposal, ranking, and panel labels

figures.data_and_statistics: This is a conceptual object with no sample size, estimator, uncertainty interval, or fitted statistic. Panel (a) encodes proposals/rankings over t=1,2,…,T; panel (b) encodes four users repeatedly ranking proposed matches around one platform.
figures.evidence_relation: PDF p.2 §1 Introduction uses Figure 1 to introduce one-shot versus long-lived users, instantaneous versus time-average utility, and the transition from online learning to equilibrium computation. The rendered object contains a PDF Form plus 52 embedded RGB/soft-mask icon objects.
design_strengths: The two panels cover both the temporal feedback interface and the multi-player equilibrium target.
Illustrative icons make the otherwise abstract ranking protocol immediately recognizable.
design_weaknesses: Many icons, arrows, formulas, and rounded boxes compete for the same page-width space.
Blue carries most process semantics and becomes weaker in grayscale; the caption does not decode the mathematical proposal notation.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a time-unrolled application panel with a multi-player feedback loop before introducing the formal regret and equilibrium definitions.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Summary of our contributions, including the negative results (top) and the positive results (bottom). The bottom table lists the minimal assumptions required to achieve sublinear regret in each setting (✓ indicates that no additional assumptions are needed). Here, τ > 0 denotes the temperature parameter of the ranking model in (PL).

tables.uncertainty: No empirical uncertainty; the cells are asymptotic rates, assumptions, and a check mark indicating no additional assumption.
tables.data_and_statistics: The upper Lower Bound subtable has InstUtil Rank Ω(T) for τ≤O(1) and AvgUtil Rank Ω̃(T)/Ω(T) conditions across full-information/bandit. The lower Upper Bound subtable lists the full-information check mark for AvgUtil Rank and Assumption 4.2, including q<1/3, for the bandit cases.
tables.evidence_relation: PDF p.3 §2 places Table 1 immediately after the contribution summary; it previews Theorems 4.1/4.3/4.4, Theorem 5.2, Theorems 6.2/6.3, and the later CCE transfer. The caption explicitly defines the top/bottom halves and ✓.
design_strengths: Negative and positive results share one ranking-feedback × information-channel matrix.
The explicit ✓ records the absence of an extra assumption instead of leaving a blank cell.
design_weaknesses: Two stacked sub-tables share a visual frame without a strong separator beyond the header text.
Ω̃, Assumption 4.2, and q<1/3 remain opaque without following the proofs; no rate constants or computational cost column is provided.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a compact theory matrix to show lower bounds, upper bounds, feedback channel, and minimum assumptions before the detailed theorem statements.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 establishes the ranking-feedback scenarios and equilibrium target; Table 1 compresses the lower/upper-bound theory matrix. Figure 2 supplies the only main-text application result, while Appendix Figures 3–6 sweep regret across feedback, temperature, variation, proposal count, and noise. Figures 7–9 transfer the evidence to game-level CCE approximation, and Figures 10–11 expose the two algorithm pipelines.
cross_object_system.caption_system: All objects use Figure n:/Table 1: prefixes. Captions generally state the feedback model and sweep parameters, but Figures 3 and 7–9 call the quantity exploitability while their y-axes read Regret or CCE Approximation: ε. Bands/95% CIs are mostly defined only in surrounding Appendix C prose, not in captions.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: The only table uses two stacked sub-tables with three logical columns and two row groups. Lower Bound and Upper Bound headers align full-information versus bandit, while bold row labels identify InstUtil Rank and AvgUtil Rank. It omits units, rate constants, and cost.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figures 10 and 11 diagram Algorithm 2/3; Figures 3–5 show their online regret behavior, Figure 6 ablates AvgUtil noise, and Figures 7–9 show game CCE. Table 1 states the theorem assumptions that delimit these curves, but no component-deletion ablation isolates estimator or exploration effects.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: The main Figure 2 application points to Appendix C for broader online-learning and equilibrium experiments. Appendix C Figures 3–9 expand the parameter/game evidence, while Appendix F Figures 10–11 pair directly with Algorithm 2/3 and fill in estimator, copy/block, and exploration dataflow.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Body, captions, and Table 1 use Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern; plot axes, legends, and diagrams use the same family of CMR/CMMI/CMSY glyphs. Figure internals shrink to roughly 3–4 pt ticks in several panels, so font family is consistent but practical size is not.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Orange/green/purple often mean τ, but blue/red mean q or K in selected panels. Deep blue in Figure 1 means illustrative flow and blue in Figures 10–11 means dashed scope boundary. Line styles provide partial redundancy, yet the paper has no global palette legend.

most_reusable_patterns: Introduce an ordinal-feedback scenario and equilibrium target with a two-panel motivation diagram.
Summarize lower bounds, upper bounds, feedback channels, and minimum assumptions in one theory matrix.
Use matched fixed-parameter sweeps for regret and then reuse the geometry for game-level CCE curves.
Hold algorithm and time axis fixed while changing only noise in an explicit ablation.
Draw full-information and bandit variants as aligned pipelines, highlighting only the feedback-specific operator.
highest_value_objects: Table 1: the clearest compact statement of the paper’s theory boundary.
Figures 10–11: the most reproducible visual specification of the two algorithm dataflows.
Figure 2: the only main-text application result and the bridge to LLM routing.
Figures 7–9: the bridge from regret to approximate CCE with repeated-run bands.
failure_patterns: Caption terminology and plotted estimand disagree: Figure 3 says exploitability but plots Regret; Figures 7–9 say exploitability but plot CCE Approximation: ε.
Most captions omit band/CI aggregation, color/line semantics, endpoint summaries, or units; very small ticks and legends reduce readability.
τ, q, and K reuse colors under different meanings, while Figure 1/10/11 use blue for non-statistical flow semantics.
No author-linked plotting or table source is publicly validated; automatic GitHub candidates are aggregators rather than visual-source repositories.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper defines ranking-feedback settings with a scenario diagram and theory matrix, then moves from LLM-routing regret through appendix sweeps and CCE curves to algorithm dataflow diagrams, linking information limits, empirical behavior, equilibrium outcomes, and implementation structure.
